title: Advanced Set-Operation Patterns
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of advanced set-operation patterns.
Apply combining multiple datasets in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn advanced set-operation patterns through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Advanced Set-Operation Patterns matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of advanced set-operation patterns is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Combining multiple datasets, Adding compatible placeholder columns, Comparing snapshots, Detecting differences between sources. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Combining multiple datasets
items.text: Combining multiple datasets helps you use scalar, correlated, and existence subqueries and combine compatible result sets without confusing set semantics or NULL behavior. items.title: Choosing set operations vs. joins
items.text: Choosing set operations vs. joins determines how rows from related sources are matched. Write the join predicate explicitly and check whether multiple matches can multiply rows; use a LEFT JOIN when unmatched left-side records must remain visible.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT full_name
FROM customers
WHERE full_name LIKE 'A%'
ORDER BY full_name;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query returns names that start with A in this PostgreSQL example; case sensitivity and regular-expression operators vary by database.

The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic combining multiple datasets and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
